# Coherent Multichannel Acquisition: Background and Theory {#coherent-multichannel-acquisition-background-and-theory}

This document explains why the HeIMDALL DAQ chain exists in the form it has. It covers what "coherent" means, which hardware impairments break coherence, what each pipeline stage does to the samples, and how the calibration loop estimates and removes each error. It ends with the limits of the model. The most important limit is that two receivers in different enclosures are never coherent with each other.

The audience is a software engineer who has not worked with antenna arrays. Every statement about this repository is taken from the source. The source file is named in the text or in a "Source:" line. Where this document and the code disagree, the code wins.

Companion documents: [architecture.md](architecture.html) (processes and IPC), [protocols.md](protocols.html) (wire formats and the header layout), [configuration.md](configuration.html) (every INI key).

## 1. Why coherence matters

A coherent receiver lets you compare the phase of one signal as seen by several antennas. All array processing depends on that comparison. If each channel adds its own unknown phase, the comparison measures the hardware instead of the signal.

### 1.1 Complex samples carry phase

Each receiver outputs complex baseband samples, also called IQ samples. A sample `x[n] = I + jQ` holds an amplitude and a phase. The phase of a narrowband signal at one antenna is meaningless on its own, because it depends on when you started counting. The phase difference between two antennas is meaningful. It depends only on geometry.

### 1.2 Direction finding

A plane wave from angle `θ` reaches two antennas spaced `d` apart at slightly different times. For a narrowband signal of wavelength `λ`, that time difference shows up as a phase difference:

```
Δφ = 2π · d · sin(θ) / λ
```

A uniform linear array of M elements produces the "steering vector" `a(θ) = [1, e^(-jΔφ), e^(-j2Δφ), ...]`. Direction-of-arrival (DoA) algorithms such as Bartlett, Capon or MUSIC search for the `θ` whose steering vector best matches the measured spatial correlation matrix.

Any per-channel phase error adds directly to `Δφ`. That turns into a bearing error.

| Quantity at 700 MHz (the default `center_freq`) | Value |
|---|---|
| Wavelength `λ = c / f` | 0.429 m |
| Half-wavelength spacing `d = λ/2` | 0.214 m |
| Bearing error at broadside per 1° of uncorrected phase error | about 0.32° |

The last row follows from `dθ = dφ / (π · cos θ)` for `d = λ/2`. A 1° phase error at broadside costs about a third of a degree. A random 0 to 360° LO phase, which is what an uncalibrated RTL-SDR array has, makes the bearing meaningless.

### 1.3 Beamforming

A beamformer multiplies each channel by a complex weight and sums. With weights matched to the steering vector, the signal from `θ` adds in phase and uncorrelated noise does not. The SNR gain (array gain) is up to M, which is 7 dB for five channels. With matched weights the coherent signal power grows as M² and the noise power as M. That gain only appears if the channel phases are known. With unknown phases the signal adds randomly and the array gain disappears.

### 1.4 Passive radar

Passive radar uses a broadcast transmitter as the illuminator. One channel (the reference) points at the transmitter. Other channels (surveillance) look at the target area. The processor computes the cross-ambiguity function between them, which is a cross-correlation over delay and Doppler shift.

This needs coherence for two reasons. First, the delay axis is measured in samples, so the channels must sample at the same instants. Second, the Doppler axis is measured in phase rotation over the integration time, so the channels must share one frequency reference. A frequency offset between channels looks like a false Doppler shift on every target. The header field `ioo_type` (illuminator of opportunity type) exists for this use case. It is copied from `[hw] ioo_type` by `rtl_daq.c`.

At the default sample rate and CPI the general resolution relations give these values:

| Quantity | Relation | Default value |
|---|---|---|
| Bistatic range resolution | `c / B`, where `B` is the illuminator's signal bandwidth, at most the 2.4 MHz sample rate | best case about 125 m |
| Doppler resolution | `1 / T_CPI`, with `T_CPI` = 0.437 s | about 2.3 Hz |
| Bistatic range-rate resolution at 700 MHz | `λ / T_CPI` | about 0.98 m/s |

The range resolution depends on the signal, not on the receiver. An FM broadcast illuminator of about 150 kHz gives about 2 km.

### 1.5 What "coherent" means in this firmware

The chain promises three things inside one unit, after calibration has locked:

| Property | Meaning | How it is achieved |
|---|---|---|
| Common time base | Sample `n` of every channel was taken at the same instant, to within a small fraction of a sample | Shared reference clock, plus integer and fractional delay calibration by sample-rate nudging (Section 5.3 and 5.4) |
| Known complex gain | Every channel has the same amplitude and phase response at the calibration point | Eigendecomposition of the spatial correlation matrix during noise-source bursts (Section 5.5) |
| Stability | Both properties hold between calibrations | Shared clock, PLL dithering disabled, periodic checks (Section 7) |

The chain does not promise anything across units. See Section 10.

## 2. The receiver chain and its impairments

Each channel is a consumer RTL-SDR: a Rafael Micro R820T or R820T2 tuner followed by a Realtek RTL2832U demodulator chip with an 8-bit ADC and a USB interface. The KrakenSDR packs five of these into one enclosure. The KerberosSDR packs four. The parts were never designed for coherent operation, so the firmware has to correct what the hardware does not guarantee.

### 2.1 One channel, end to end

```
antenna -> [R820T: LNA, mixer with PLL LO, IF filter, gain stages]
        -> [RTL2832U: 8-bit ADC, digital down-conversion, resampler to the output rate]
        -> USB bulk transfers of interleaved 8-bit I/Q bytes
        -> host: librtlsdr async read callback
```

The tuner mixes the RF signal down to an intermediate frequency using a local oscillator (LO). The LO is generated by a fractional-N phase-locked loop (PLL) that is locked to the crystal reference. The RTL2832U digitises the IF, shifts it to baseband and resamples it to the configured `sample_rate`. The host receives unsigned bytes, two per complex sample.

### 2.2 Impairments

Each row is something that differs between channels, or something that destroys the comparison between them.

| Impairment | Physical cause | Effect on the samples | How the firmware handles it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Independent LO phase | Each tuner has its own PLL. All PLLs lock to the same reference, so the frequencies match, but each PLL locks with an arbitrary phase | A constant phase offset per channel. It is re-randomised on every retune | Measured and removed by IQ calibration. A frequency change forces recalibration (Section 7.4) |
| PLL phase wander | Fractional-N PLLs use dithering to spread spurs, which makes the loop phase wander | Slow phase drift between channels | `rtl_daq.c` calls `rtlsdr_set_dithering(dev, 0)` for every tuner. The code comment reads "Disable dithering (To avoid phase drift)" |
| Sample-time offset | Each RTL2832U starts streaming when its own async read starts. The starts are not simultaneous | An integer offset of up to thousands of samples, plus a fractional part | Integer and fractional delay calibration (Sections 5.3 and 5.4) |
| USB transfer jitter and loss | Each dongle delivers transfers on its own schedule. A slow host can fall behind | Transfers arrive at different times. A lost or overwritten transfer shifts one channel by a whole block | `rtl_daq` aligns channels by transfer count, not by arrival time. Overwrites are detected and counted (Section 3.2) |
| 8-bit quantisation | The RTL2832U ADC has 8 bits | About 50 dB ideal signal-to-quantisation-noise ratio for a full-scale sine (`6.02·8 + 1.76`). Strong signals clip | Overdrive detection per channel. Optional gain auto-tuning (`en_gain_tune_init`) |
| Discrete gain steps | The R820T offers 29 gain settings from 0 to 49.6 dB | Each gain setting has its own amplitude and phase response | Calibration runs at a fixed gain per frequency band (Section 7.5). This is a known limitation |
| Amplitude mismatch | Gain spread between parts, cable loss | Different signal levels per channel | Amplitude correction from the eigenvector or from channel powers (Section 5.5) |
| Path outside the calibration point | Antenna cables and external LNAs between the antenna and the noise injection point | Phase and amplitude error that the noise source cannot see | Optional `iq_adjust` vector from cable delays or Touchstone files (Section 5.6) |
| Frequency-dependent response | Filters and cables have a phase response that varies across the band | A residual time delay shows up as a phase slope across the band | Fractional delay calibration (Section 5.4) |

The R820T gain table lives in `hw_controller.py` as `valid_gains`, in tenths of a dB:

```
0, 9, 14, 27, 37, 77, 87, 125, 144, 157, 166, 197, 207, 229, 254,
280, 297, 328, 338, 364, 372, 386, 402, 421, 434, 439, 445, 480, 496
```

### 2.3 The shared reference clock and the noise source

Two hardware features make calibration possible. The firmware depends on both.

**Shared reference clock.** All tuners and ADCs in one KrakenSDR or KerberosSDR run from one reference oscillator. Therefore every channel has exactly the same LO frequency and the same sample rate. The remaining differences are constant offsets: LO phase, sample-time offset and complex gain. A constant offset can be measured once and removed. A frequency difference cannot, because it produces a phase that rotates continuously. This is the whole reason one enclosure can be coherent and two enclosures cannot.

**Switched noise source.** The board has a wideband noise source that can be coupled into all inputs at once. When it is on, every channel receives the same random signal. A random wideband signal has a sharp autocorrelation peak, so it is ideal for delay estimation. Because the signal is common to all inputs, any difference between the channels is the receiver's own error.

The firmware drives the noise source through GPIO 0 of the control-channel dongle with `rtlsdr_set_bias_tee_gpio(dev, 0, state)`. The control channel is the tuner whose serial matches `[daq] ctr_channel_serial_no` (default `1000`). Per-channel bias tees use GPIO `m+1` on the same dongle, so they never collide with the noise source. Runtime bias-tee changes are deferred while a noise burst is active. The noise source is only switched when `[daq] en_noise_source_ctr = 1`.

Source: `Firmware/_daq_core/rtl_daq.c` (tuner initialisation, noise-source switch, `'b'` handler).

On KrakenSDR hardware the antennas are isolated while the noise source is on, so calibration does not need manual intervention. For setups where the antennas must be detached by hand, `hw_controller.py` supports `require_track_lock_intervention = 1`. It then waits for a `1` in the file `_data_control/iq_track_lock` (`_data_control/inst{N}_iq_track_lock` for a federation instance N > 0) before it switches the noise source off and lets the chain enter tracking. The gate applies after every full calibration, not only the first. The code never clears the file, so a `1` stays an approval. Source: `Firmware/_daq_core/hw_controller.py`.

Note that `rtl_daq` labels frames as calibration frames from its internal noise-source state, whether or not `en_noise_source_ctr` is set. With `en_noise_source_ctr = 0` the chain still runs the calibration sequence, but the GPIO is never toggled. Calibration then uses whatever signal reaches the inputs.

## 3. Pipeline stages and what each does to the data

The chain is a pipeline of processes. Each stage hands frames to the next through a pipe or a double-buffered shared-memory ring. Every frame is a 1024-byte header followed by the payload.

```
rtl_daq.out ──pipe──> rebuffer.out ──shm──> decimate.out ──shm──> delay_sync.py ──shm──> iq_server.out or shmem consumer
   ▲                                                                   │
   │ ZMQ :1130 ('s' rate nudge from delay_sync;                        │ header-only shm ring
   │  'g', 'n', 'c', 'a', 'b' from hw_controller)                      ▼
   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── hw_controller.py
```

### 3.1 Data representation at each hop

| Hop | Sample format | Samples per channel per frame | `data_type` | `sample_bit_depth` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| rtl_daq to rebuffer | interleaved uint8 I/Q | `daq_buffer_size` (one DAQ block) | 1 (DATA/CAL), 0 (DUMMY) | 8 |
| rebuffer to decimate | interleaved uint8 I/Q | DATA: `cpi_size × decimation_ratio`. CAL: `corr_size` | unchanged | 8 |
| decimate to delay_sync | complex float32 | DATA: `cpi_size`. CAL: `corr_size` | 3 | 32 |
| delay_sync to output | complex float32, corrected | same as input | 3 | 32 |

Channel blocks are stored one after another (channel 0 block, then channel 1 block, and so on), not interleaved between channels.

### 3.2 rtl_daq: acquisition and block alignment

`rtl_daq.out` opens one tuner per channel by its EEPROM serial. By default channel `i` is the dongle with serial `1000+i`. The optional `[hw] serial_base` and `[hw] device_serials` keys change that mapping. It initialises each tuner with dithering off, manual gain mode, the configured centre frequency, gain and sample rate. It then starts one USB reader thread per channel with `rtlsdr_read_async`. Each USB transfer is `2 × daq_buffer_size` bytes.

The reader callback copies each transfer into a ring of `[daq] usb_ring_buffers` slots per channel (default 8, range 2 to 64) and increments that channel's transfer counter. The main loop waits until every channel's counter is past the current read index. It then emits one frame that contains block number `k` from every channel. This is how channels are aligned at the block level: by counting transfers, not by time.

This alignment has a consequence. If one channel loses a transfer, or if the readers lap the ring, the channels are shifted by a whole block against each other. `rtl_daq` detects the lap case. It counts the affected frames and stamps the running total into header slot `reserved[102]` (`IQH_RSV_BUFFER_OVERRUN_CNT`). The frame is still emitted, and the sync flags are not cleared. A consumer that needs guaranteed coherence should watch this counter and discard frames while it increases.

For each frame, `rtl_daq` also:

- stamps `time_stamp` in milliseconds since the Unix epoch, from `gettimeofday` (wall clock, not monotonic);
- stamps `daq_block_index`, the block counter;
- sets `adc_overdrive_flags` bit `i` when channel `i` contains any byte equal to 255;
- copies `rf_center_freq`, `if_gains[]` and `noise_source_state`;
- sets `frame_type` to CAL when the noise source is on, DATA otherwise, and DUMMY during the settle period after a command.

**Dummy frames.** Every control command that `rtl_daq` receives on ZMQ (gain, frequency, noise source, rate nudge and the others) sets a flag that makes the next five frames header-only DUMMY frames (`NO_DUMMY_FRAMES 5`). Acquisition continues, but the payload is dropped. This gives the tuners time to settle. Rebuffer and `delay_sync` use DUMMY frames as a reset marker. Decimate does not (Section 3.4).

**Applying commands.** Tuner changes are applied between frames, after a frame has been written. The `'s'` rate correction has special timing, described in Section 5.4.

Source: `Firmware/_daq_core/rtl_daq.c`.

### 3.3 rebuffer: from DAQ blocks to processing frames

`rebuffer.out` changes the frame size. USB transfers have a fixed size (`daq_buffer_size`). Processing wants a different size: `cpi_size × decimation_ratio` samples for DATA, `corr_size` samples for CAL. Rebuffer keeps a per-channel circular buffer and emits an output frame when enough samples have accumulated for the current frame type.

| Input frame | Action |
|---|---|
| DUMMY | Clear all circular buffers and offsets. Forward the header with `cpi_length = 0` |
| DATA or CAL | Append the block. Emit a frame when `corr_size` (CAL) or `cpi_size × decimation_ratio` (DATA) samples are available |

Rebuffer also ORs the overdrive flags of all blocks that went into a frame. It corrects `time_stamp` backwards by the duration of the samples still waiting in the buffer. `time_stamp` then marks the arrival of the frame's last sample, plus USB latency. The first sample is about `cpi_size × decimation_ratio / adc_sampling_freq` earlier, 437 ms at the defaults.

Because a DUMMY frame clears the buffer, the first frame after any command contains only samples taken after that command. That is what makes the calibration loop's measure, nudge, measure cycle clean.

Source: `Firmware/_daq_core/rebuffer.c`.

### 3.4 decimate: format conversion and FIR decimation

`decimate.out` converts uint8 samples to float with `(x − 127.5) / 127.5`, so the full ADC range maps to [−1, 1]. It then branches on the frame type:

| Frame | `decimation_ratio` | Processing | Output rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| DATA | > 1 | Low-pass FIR filter and keep every R-th sample | `adc_sampling_freq / R` |
| DATA | = 1 | Conversion only, no filtering | `adc_sampling_freq` |
| CAL | any | Conversion only, no filtering or decimation | `adc_sampling_freq` |

Calibration therefore always runs at the full ADC rate, where one sample is the smallest unit of delay. The FIR is identical for every channel. It adds the same group delay and the same phase response to every channel, so it does not change the relative phase or delay between channels. That is why it is safe to calibrate before the filter and apply the result after it.

The FIR state (the last `fir_tap_size − 1` input samples) carries over from one DATA frame to the next, so the output is a continuous filtered stream. Setting `en_filter_reset = 1` clears the state before every frame instead.

DUMMY frames do not reset the FIR state. Rebuffer drops samples around every command, so the input is not continuous across a DUMMY gap. With `decimation_ratio > 1` and `en_filter_reset = 0`, the first `fir_tap_size − 1` input samples of the first DATA frame after a command are filtered together with stale samples from before the gap. After a retune those samples have a different LO phase, and after a gain change a different gain. Discard that many samples, or set `en_filter_reset = 1`. Source: `Firmware/_daq_core/fir_decimate.c`.

`decimate.out` also sets `cpi_index`, a counter of frames it has processed, including DUMMY frames.

Source: `Firmware/_daq_core/fir_decimate.c`, `Firmware/_daq_core/offload_cpu_generic.c`.

**FIR design.** `fir_filter_designer.py` runs at every start. It writes the taps to `_data_control/fir_coeffs.txt`, which `decimate.out` reads once at start-up. The design is a windowed-sinc low-pass filter:

```python
cut_off = fir_relative_bandwidth / decimation_ratio
if cut_off < 1:
    b = scipy.signal.firwin(fir_tap_size, cut_off, window=fir_window)
else:
    b = [1]
```

`firwin` measures the cut-off as a fraction of the input Nyquist frequency, and the cut-off is the −6 dB point of the response. With `fir_relative_bandwidth = 1.0` the −6 dB point lands exactly on the output Nyquist frequency. Signal energy just above that point folds back into the band (aliasing). A value below 1.0 trades usable bandwidth for less aliasing. More taps give a sharper transition.

Example with `sample_rate = 2400000`, `decimation_ratio = 4`, `fir_relative_bandwidth = 0.8`:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Output sample rate | 600 kHz |
| Output Nyquist frequency | 300 kHz |
| Cut-off (−6 dB) | `0.8 / 4 = 0.2` of input Nyquist = 240 kHz |

The designer rejects `decimation_ratio < 1` and `fir_tap_size <= decimation_ratio` when the ratio is not 1. `ini_checker.py` enforces the same rule. The default configuration uses `decimation_ratio = 1` and `fir_tap_size = 1`, so the filter is bypassed.

Source: `Firmware/fir_filter_designer.py`.

### 3.5 delay_sync: calibration and correction

`delay_sync.py` is where coherence is established. It runs the calibration state machine on CAL frames (Sections 5 and 6). It sends rate nudges to `rtl_daq`. It applies the amplitude and phase corrections to every frame. It stamps the sync flags and `sync_state` into the header.

The correction it applies to the output is:

```python
out[m, :] = (in[m, :] - mean(in[m, :])) * iq_corrections[m]
```

So when `en_iq_cal = 1`, every frame has its per-channel DC component removed and is multiplied by one complex number per channel. When `en_iq_cal = 0`, the samples are copied unchanged. In that case the output is time-aligned but carries the raw LO phases.

Integer and fractional delay are never corrected in software. There is no sample shifting or interpolation anywhere in the chain. Alignment is achieved physically, by speeding up or slowing down the tuners' sample clocks until the streams line up.

Source: `Firmware/_daq_core/delay_sync.py` (`correct_iq`, `copy_iq`).

### 3.6 hw_controller: the control loop

`hw_controller.py` reads only the header of every frame, from a header-only ring that `delay_sync` fills. It decides when the noise source is on, sets calibration and operating gains, and serves the TCP control port 5001. It is the only process that sends the noise-source command. Without it, no calibration bursts happen.

## 4. Worked numbers at the default configuration

These values are computed from `Firmware/daq_chain_config.ini` (preset `kraken_default`) and the frame sizes in the code.

| Parameter | INI key | Default |
|---|---|---|
| Channels M | `[hw] num_ch` | 5 |
| ADC output sample rate | `[daq] sample_rate` | 2 400 000 samples/s |
| DAQ block | `[daq] daq_buffer_size` | 262 144 samples (2^18) |
| CPI size (after decimation) | `[pre_processing] cpi_size` | 1 048 576 samples (2^20) |
| Decimation ratio R | `[pre_processing] decimation_ratio` | 1 |
| Correlation (CAL frame) size | `[calibration] corr_size` | 65 536 samples (2^16) |
| Burst interval | `[calibration] cal_frame_interval` | 687 frames |
| Burst size | `[calibration] cal_frame_burst_size` | 10 frames |
| Max sync fails | `[calibration] maximum_sync_fails` | 10 |
| Tracking mode | `[calibration] cal_track_mode` | 2 |

Derived timing:

| Quantity | Formula | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Sample period | `1 / fs` | 416.7 ns |
| DAQ block period | `daq_buffer_size / fs` | 109.2 ms (9.16 blocks/s) |
| CPI duration (DATA frame period) | `cpi_size × R / fs` | 436.9 ms (2.29 frames/s) |
| DAQ blocks per DATA frame | `cpi_size × R / daq_buffer_size` | 4 |
| CAL frame span | `corr_size / fs` | 27.3 ms |
| Time between calibration bursts | `687 × 436.9 ms` | about 300 s (5 minutes) |
| Dummy settle period after a command | `5 × 109.2 ms` | 546 ms |

Derived data volume:

| Quantity | Formula | Value |
|---|---|---|
| USB rate per channel | `2 bytes × fs` | 4.8 MB/s |
| USB rate, all channels | `5 × 4.8 MB/s` | 24 MB/s |
| rtl_daq frame size | `1024 + 5 × 2 × 262 144` | 2 622 464 bytes |
| DATA frame after decimate | `1024 + 5 × 8 × 1 048 576` | 41 944 064 bytes (40.0 MiB) |
| Output stream rate (float32 complex) | `5 × 8 bytes × fs / R` | 96 MB/s |
| CAL frame after decimate | `1024 + 5 × 8 × 65 536` | 2 622 464 bytes |

Calibration resolution:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Fractional delay tolerance `0.03` samples | 12.5 ns |
| Phase error across the band from a 0.03-sample residual, at the band edge (`360° × 0.5 × 0.03`) | 5.4° |
| Correlation peak sidelobe probe offset (100 samples) | 41.7 µs |
| Ideal correlation processing gain over `corr_size` (`10·log10(65536)`) | 48 dB |

The output stream rate shows why `decimation_ratio` is the main capacity lever. Float32 complex samples are four times larger than the USB bytes. With R = 4 the output rate falls to 24 MB/s.

## 5. Calibration theory

Calibration estimates three errors per channel, relative to a reference channel `std_ch_ind` (default 0):

1. an integer sample offset;
2. a fractional sample offset;
3. a complex gain (amplitude and phase).

The first two are removed by nudging the hardware sample clock. The third is removed by multiplying the samples.

### 5.1 Signal model

While the noise source is on, channel `m` receives:

```
x_m[n] = g_m · s[n − τ_m] + w_m[n]
```

- `s[n]` is the common noise signal.
- `τ_m` is the channel's time offset in samples, integer plus fraction.
- `g_m` is the channel's complex gain. Its phase includes the LO phase.
- `w_m[n]` is the channel's own receiver noise, independent between channels.

Calibration first drives `τ_m − τ_ref` to zero. Then it estimates `g_m / g_ref` and multiplies channel `m` by the inverse.

### 5.2 Noise-source bursts and CAL frames

A calibration burst is a period when the noise source is on. `hw_controller.py` starts one by:

1. saving the operating gains and AGC state;
2. setting every channel to the calibration gain for the current frequency (Section 7.5);
3. sending the `'n'` (noise on) command to `rtl_daq`.

`rtl_daq` then marks frames as CAL. Rebuffer emits CAL frames of `corr_size` samples. Decimate passes them through at the full rate. When the burst ends, `hw_controller` sends noise off and restores the saved gains and AGC state.

Every command produces five DUMMY frames, one per DAQ block. Rebuffer emits one CAL frame per DAQ block (`corr_size ≤ daq_buffer_size`), not one per CPI. `hw_controller`'s burst state machine runs only on non-DUMMY frames: the first CAL frame only clears `STATE_NOISE_CTR_WAIT` and is not counted, and the 10th counted frame triggers noise off. A periodic burst therefore costs 5 DUMMY + at least 11 CAL + 5 DUMMY blocks, plus the 1 or 2 blocks of the partial CPI that rebuffer discards: about 22 to 24 blocks of 109.2 ms. That is 2.4 to 2.6 s of lost samples and a gap of 2.9 to 3.1 s between DATA frames, every ≈302 s (about 0.8 to 0.9 % duty cycle). These are derived from the code, not measured. To measure, log `frame_type` and `time_stamp` across one burst.

CAL frames are forwarded to the output like any other frame. A consumer must check `frame_type` and use only DATA frames (`frame_type = 0`) for signal processing.

### 5.3 Integer delay: cross-correlation

**Point:** the peak of the cross-correlation between a channel and the reference sits at their relative delay.

For each non-reference channel, `delay_sync` computes the cross-correlation of the first `corr_size` samples with the reference channel. It zero-pads both to `2 × corr_size` (the reference as `[x, 0]`, the other channel as `[0, y]`) so that the circular FFT correlation does not wrap. The squared magnitude of the result is the correlation function:

```python
X = FFT([x_ref, zeros])
Y = FFT([zeros, x_m])
corr_m = |IFFT(conj(X) · Y)|^2
peak_index = argmax(corr_m)
delay_m = corr_size − peak_index
```

The sign is the reverse of what you might expect. If `y[n] = x[n − d]` (channel m late by `d`), the peak is at `corr_size + d`, so `delay_m = −d`. `delay_m > 0` means channel m leads the reference. A late channel gives a negative `delay_m` and receives a positive rate offset. Source: `Firmware/_daq_core/delay_sync.py`, derivation in `synth_model.py`.

**Quality gate.** The noise source is wideband, so its correlation peak is narrow. The code checks the ratio of the peak to the value 100 samples away:

```
dyn_range = 10 · log10(corr[peak] / corr[(peak + 100) mod (2 · corr_size)])
```

Every non-reference channel must reach at least 20 dB (`min_corr_peak_dyn_range`). If one channel fails, the code logs a warning, sends no correction and waits for the next CAL frame. A failure usually means the noise source is off, too weak, or swamped by a strong external signal. There is no timeout. A chain that never sees a good correlation stays in `sync_state` 2 with the noise source on.

For comparison, two fully correlated white-noise records of 65 536 samples give a peak about 48 dB above the typical sidelobe. The 20 dB gate leaves a wide margin.

**Correction.** If any channel has a non-zero delay, `delay_sync` computes one rate offset per channel:

```python
gain = 50 if |delay| >= 100 else (25 if |delay| >= 2 else 15)
fs_offset[m] = −delay_m · gain · 1e-7          # MIN_FS_PPM_OFFSET = 1e-7
fs_offset[m] = clip(fs_offset[m], −0.01, +0.01)  # MAX_FS_PPM_OFFSET = 0.01
```

It sends the offsets to `rtl_daq` as one `'s'` message of float32 values. When all delays are zero, the integer stage is done.

Source: `Firmware/_daq_core/delay_sync.py` (`STATE_SAMPLE_CAL`).

### 5.4 Fractional delay: sample-rate nudging

**Point:** if you run one channel's sample clock slightly fast for a known time, it gains a known number of samples on the others.

The RTL2832U output rate comes from a digital resampler. The krakenrf fork of librtlsdr exposes a fine rate correction, `rtlsdr_set_sample_freq_correction_f`. That library is outside this repository. The code calls the value a "ppm" offset, but its magnitude (1e-7 to 1e-2) only works as a fractional rate offset: a value of `v` makes the channel produce `v × N` extra samples over `N` samples. The design notes for the synthetic test model use the same interpretation. The exact loop gains need characterisation on hardware.

**Timing in rtl_daq.** The `'s'` command is applied after the next frame is written. After the frame following that, each channel's correction is reset to 0, unless `|value| >= 0.008` (`FS_CORRECTION_KEEP_LIMIT`). So a small correction is active for about one DAQ block. A large correction stays active until the next `'s'` command replaces it.

**Expected slip per command.** With `daq_buffer_size = 2^18` and a correction held for one block, the slip is `v × 262 144` samples:

| Measured delay | Gain | Offset `v` | Slip per command | Loop gain (slip / delay) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 15 | 1.5e-6 | 0.39 samples | 0.39 |
| 10 | 25 | 2.5e-5 | 6.6 samples | 0.66 |
| 50 | 25 | 1.25e-4 | 32.8 samples | 0.66 |
| 150 | 50 | 7.5e-4 | 197 samples | 1.31 |
| ≥ 1600 | 50 | ≥ 0.008 | kept until the next `'s'`, about 5 to 6 blocks: ≥ 10 000 samples | far above 2 for delays below about 10 000 |

A loop gain below 1 converges without overshoot. A loop gain between 1 and 2 overshoots and still converges. Under this model a one-sample delay takes about two commands (residual 0.61, then 0.21 samples); hardware convergence is not characterised (design gap G67). The fractional stage removes the rest.

A kept correction stays on until the next `'s'`. That command only comes after the 5 DUMMY frames and the first CAL frame, so the correction runs for about 5 to 6 blocks. Under this model it overshoots any delay below about 10 000 samples, so the model predicts oscillation. Hardware converges, so the model is incomplete for large corrections. Treat these numbers as unverified until they are characterised on hardware (design gap G67). The gains are hard-coded and are not scaled by `daq_buffer_size`, so a much larger block raises every loop gain in proportion. Large blocks can make the loop oscillate.

**Wait states.** After sending `'s'`, `delay_sync` enters `STATE_SYNC_WAIT`. It leaves on the first DUMMY frame, which the command itself caused. Rebuffer has cleared its buffer at that point, so the next CAL frame contains only post-correction samples.

**Fractional estimate.** Once the integer delay is zero, a residual below one sample remains. A time delay `τ` multiplies the spectrum by `e^(−j2π f τ)`, which is a phase that grows linearly with frequency. `estimate_frac_delays` measures that slope:

1. Split the reference and channel `m` into blocks of 1024 samples and FFT each block.
2. Remove the constant phase between the channels, estimated as `mean(x_ref · conj(x_m))`.
3. Average the ratio `X_ref / X_m` over all blocks (64 blocks for `corr_size = 65536`).
4. Take the phase angle at each frequency bin.
5. Fit a straight line over normalised frequencies `−0.4 < f < 0.4`, which skips the band edges.
6. The delay in samples is `slope / (2π)`.

If any `|τ| > 0.03` samples (`frac_delay_tolerance`), the code sends `'s'` with, for each channel `m` whose `|τ| > 0.03`:

```python
fs_offset[m] = sign(τ) · |τ| · 20 · 1e-7      # FRAC_FS_TUNE_GAIN = 20
```

Channels with `|τ| ≤ 0.03` and the reference channel get 0 (`frac_fs_ppm_offsets`). That is a loop gain of about 0.52 at the default block size. It then waits in `STATE_FRAC_SYNC_WAIT` for a DUMMY frame, exactly like the integer stage. When every residual is within 0.03 samples, it moves to IQ calibration.

Source: `Firmware/_daq_core/delay_sync.py` (`estimate_frac_delays`, `STATE_FRAC_SAMPLE_CAL`), `Firmware/_daq_core/rtl_daq.c` (`'s'` handler and `FS_CORRECTION_KEEP_LIMIT`).

### 5.5 Amplitude and phase: eigendecomposition

**Point:** when every channel sees the same signal, the dominant eigenvector of the spatial correlation matrix is the vector of channel gains.

After alignment, the model is `x[n] = g · s[n] + w[n]`, where `x` and `g` are M-element vectors. The spatial correlation matrix is:

```
R_xx = E[x · x^H] = σ_s² · g · g^H + σ_w² · I
```

This assumes equal receiver noise power in every channel. With unequal noise the estimate is biased, by an amount on the order of the noise-to-signal ratio. The noise source is strong, so the bias is small. `calc_iq_sync` does no noise whitening.

The first term has rank one, and its only eigenvector with a non-zero eigenvalue is `g`. Adding `σ_w² · I` shifts every eigenvalue up and leaves the eigenvectors unchanged. So the eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue is `g` up to a scale factor. That is exactly the set of complex gains the calibration needs, and it uses every channel pair at once.

`calc_iq_sync` implements this:

```python
Rxx = X @ X.conj().T                 # X: M x corr_size
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = numpy.linalg.eigh(Rxx)
v_max = eigenvectors[:, -1]          # eigh sorts ascending
iq_diffs = 1 / v_max
iq_diffs /= iq_diffs[std_ch_ind]     # reference channel = 1
```

`iq_diffs[m]` is the complex factor that makes channel `m` match the reference. The amplitude part depends on `amplitude_cal_mode`:

| Mode | Phase | Amplitude |
|---|---|---|
| `default` | from the eigenvector | from the eigenvector |
| `channel_power` (default INI) | from the eigenvector | `sqrt(P_ref / P_m)`, from measured channel powers |
| `disabled` | from the eigenvector | none (unit magnitude) |

The same function also computes a correlation check at lag 0 against lag 100 for each channel. A channel that has lost sample alignment fails this check.

**Iteration.** In `STATE_IQ_CAL`, each CAL frame is measured after the current corrections have been applied. If any channel's phase exceeds `phase_tolerance` degrees, or its magnitude exceeds `10^(amplitude_tolerance/20)`, the corrections are updated by multiplication, `iq_corrections *= iq_diffs`, and the next CAL frame is measured. When all channels are within tolerance, calibration locks. Two details:

- Both tolerances are read with `getint`, so they are whole numbers (default 1° and 2 dB).
- The amplitude check only flags a magnitude above the limit, not below it.

If the correlation check fails in this state, sample alignment is assumed lost, and the state machine returns to the integer stage. With `en_iq_cal = 0` there is no check: the state locks on its first frame.

Source: `Firmware/_daq_core/delay_sync.py` (`calc_iq_sync`, `STATE_IQ_CAL`).

### 5.6 Correcting the path outside the calibration point

The noise source enters each channel at some point inside the receiver. Everything between the antenna and that point, mainly the antenna cables, is invisible to calibration. Two cables that differ in length by a few centimetres add a phase difference that calibration cannot see.

The `iq_adjust` vector compensates for that. It is applied on top of the measured corrections. After convergence the corrected channels differ at the injection point by `iq_adjust`, within the calibration tolerances. Two sources are supported (`[calibration] iq_adjust_source`):

| Source | Input | Conversion |
|---|---|---|
| `explicit-time-delay` | `iq_adjust_amplitude` (dB) and `iq_adjust_time_delay_ns` (ns), one value per non-reference channel | `amplitude = 10^(dB/20)`, `phase = 2π · f_RF · τ` |
| `touchstone` | `_calibration/cable_ch{m}.s1p` per channel | The file's single parameter at the frequency point closest to `f_RF`, used as the transmission coefficient |

The vector is normalised to the reference channel. It is recomputed in `STATE_INIT` from the current `rf_center_freq`, because a fixed time delay becomes a different phase at every frequency. For example, a 1 ns cable difference is 252° of phase at 700 MHz.

Two sign and format rules matter:

- A positive `iq_adjust_time_delay_ns` means channel m's path outside the calibration point is longer (later) than the reference path.
- The code uses the single parameter of each `.s1p` file as the path's transmission coefficient (S21). Export S21 of a two-port cable measurement into the `.s1p` file. A reflection (S11) measurement of a terminated cable gives twice the phase and the loss squared, which is wrong here.

An external LNA is also outside the calibration point. Its gain and phase differences between units are invisible to calibration (Section 8.2).

---

## 6. The sync state machine

`delay_sync.py` runs a state machine with eight internal states. It reports them in the header field `sync_state` as the values 1 to 6, because three states share the value 3. A DUMMY frame always carries 0, whatever the state.

| `sync_state` | Internal state | What happens | `delay_sync_flag` / `iq_sync_flag` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | any, on a DUMMY frame | Frame not processed. The fail counter is reset | 0 / 0 |
| 1 | `STATE_INIT` | Recompute `iq_adjust`. Reset the corrections to `iq_adjust`. Wait for the first CAL frame | 0 / 0 |
| 2 | `STATE_SAMPLE_CAL` | Integer delay estimation and `'s'` nudges (Section 5.3) | `delay_sync_flag` 1 only when every delay is 0. `iq_sync_flag` 0 |
| 3 | `STATE_SYNC_WAIT` | Wait for the DUMMY frame caused by the integer nudge | 0 / 0 |
| 3 | `STATE_FRAC_SAMPLE_CAL` | Fractional delay estimation and nudges (Section 5.4) | 0 / 0 |
| 3 | `STATE_FRAC_SYNC_WAIT` | Wait for the DUMMY frame caused by the fractional nudge | 0 / 0 |
| 4 | `STATE_IQ_CAL` | Amplitude and phase estimation and correction (Section 5.5) | 1 / 1 when in tolerance. 1 / 0 while corrections are updated. 0 / 0 when the correlation check fails |
| 5 | `STATE_TRACK_LOCK` | Locked. Wait for the first DATA frame, which means the burst has ended | 1 / 1 |
| 6 | `STATE_TRACK` | Locked and tracking (Section 7) | 1 / 1 unless a check on this frame fails |

The normal path is:

```
1 INIT ──CAL frame──> 2 SAMPLE_CAL ──delays≠0──> 3 SYNC_WAIT ──DUMMY──> 2 SAMPLE_CAL
                          │ all delays 0
                          ▼
                      3 FRAC_SAMPLE_CAL ──|τ|>0.03──> 3 FRAC_SYNC_WAIT ──DUMMY──> 3 FRAC_SAMPLE_CAL
                          │ all |τ| ≤ 0.03
                          ▼
                      4 IQ_CAL ──out of tolerance: update, stay──┐
                          │ in tolerance          ▲──────────────┘
                          │ correlation check fails ──> 2 SAMPLE_CAL
                          ▼
                      5 TRACK_LOCK ──first DATA frame──> 6 TRACK
                                                           │ fail limit or RF change
                                                           ▼
                                                        1 INIT
```

`hw_controller.py` keys off `sync_state` from the header:

- `sync_state < 5`: turn the noise source on if it is off.
- `sync_state >= 5`: turn the noise source off if it is on (modes 0 and 1, and mode 2 outside a burst).
- `sync_state == 6`: count frames toward the next burst (mode 2).

The status server reports `calibration_status` as `locked` for `sync_state >= 5`, `calibrating` for 2 to 4, and `lost` otherwise. DUMMY frames carry `sync_state` 0 even while the chain is locked. A single sample of `sync_state` is therefore not a reliable health signal. Look at several consecutive non-DUMMY frames.

**What a consumer should accept.** A DATA frame is safe for coherent processing when `frame_type == 0`, `delay_sync_flag == 1`, `iq_sync_flag == 1` and `sync_state >= 5`, and when the overrun counter in `reserved[102]` has not changed since the previous frame. In mode 2 the flags on DATA frames repeat the result of the last burst. They are not a measurement on that frame (Section 7.1).

---

## 7. Tracking, drift and recalibration

Once locked, the corrections are frozen. `STATE_TRACK` never updates `iq_corrections` and never sends `'s'`. It only checks whether the lock still holds. When the check fails often enough, the chain discards the lock and runs a full calibration from `STATE_INIT`.

### 7.1 Tracking modes: `cal_track_mode`

| Mode | Noise source after lock | What `STATE_TRACK` checks | Reference for the check |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | Off, permanently | Nothing. Only an RF frequency change triggers recalibration | none |
| 1 | Off, permanently | Every DATA frame | `iq_diffs` measured on the first DATA frame after lock |
| 2 (default) | Periodic bursts | CAL frames of each burst only. DATA frames pass with the flags set | `iq_diffs` measured when IQ calibration locked |

On each checked frame, the check fails when:

- any channel's lag-0 against lag-100 correlation ratio is below 20 dB (sample alignment lost); or
- with `en_iq_cal = 1`, any channel's `iq_diffs / iq_diff_ref` exceeds the phase or amplitude tolerance.

**Mode 0** suits short sessions and lab work. It has no drift detection at all.

**Mode 1** measures the live signal. Both checks assume that the received field is wideband and does not change. A narrowband signal has a broad autocorrelation, so the lag-100 value can be as large as the lag-0 value. A moving or changing source changes the eigenvector. Either effect counts as a failure. Mode 1 therefore only makes sense when the received signal is stable and wideband, for example a fixed reference transmitter or a test feed.

**Mode 2** checks against the noise source, which is the same signal every time. `hw_controller` counts frames while `sync_state == 6`. At `cal_frame_interval` frames it starts a burst. At `cal_frame_interval + cal_frame_burst_size` it ends the burst and resets the count.

### 7.2 The fail counter

The counter is a net count within one burst:

- a failed check adds 1;
- a passing check subtracts 1, with a floor of 0;
- a DUMMY frame resets it to 0;
- when it reaches `maximum_sync_fails`, the lock is dropped and the state returns to `STATE_INIT`.

The noise-on command at the start of a burst produces DUMMY frames, so the counter starts at 0 for every burst. In mode 2 the counter can therefore only reach the limit if one burst has at least `maximum_sync_fails` more failing CAL frames than passing ones. If `maximum_sync_fails` is larger than the number of CAL frames in a burst, mode 2 can never detect a loss. Keep `maximum_sync_fails` at or below `cal_frame_burst_size`. With the defaults (both 10), every CAL frame of a burst must fail to drop the lock. Lower `maximum_sync_fails` for faster detection.

When the lock is dropped during a burst, the noise source is still on. `hw_controller` sees `sync_state < 5` and leaves it on. Full calibration then runs on the same burst.

### 7.3 What makes sync drift

| Cause | What drifts | Detected by |
|---|---|---|
| Retune | LO phase re-randomised on every tuner | RF-change check (immediate recalibration) |
| Temperature change | Tuner gain and phase, crystal and PLL behaviour | Mode 1 or 2 phase and amplitude check |
| Lost or overwritten USB transfer | Whole-block shift between channels | Correlation check in mode 1 or 2, at the next checked frame. The overrun counter in `reserved[102]` shows it at once |
| Gain change | Gain-dependent phase response | Not detected in modes 0 and 2 (mode-2 bursts run at the calibration gain). In mode 1 it can trip the phase and amplitude check, because the reference was taken at the old operating gain |
| Large residual rate correction | A correction of `>= 0.008` stays active and keeps slipping | Correlation check |
| Cable or antenna change | Path outside the calibration point | Never detected by the noise source. Update `iq_adjust` |

### 7.4 Recalibration triggers

| Trigger | Where | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `rf_center_freq` differs from the value at lock | `delay_sync` `STATE_TRACK` | `STATE_INIT`, so full calibration |
| Fail counter reaches `maximum_sync_fails` | `delay_sync` `STATE_TRACK` | `STATE_INIT`, so full calibration |
| Correlation check fails in `STATE_IQ_CAL` | `delay_sync` | Back to `STATE_SAMPLE_CAL` |
| `INIT` on port 5001 | `hw_controller` only | Re-enters `hw_controller`'s `STATE_INIT`: re-applies the current gains (the last applied `GAIN`, not the INI `[daq] gain`), sends noise off. Deferred while a calibration burst is active. There is no path into `delay_sync`, so a locked chain stays locked |
| `RECL` on port 5001 with `[calibration] en_wire_recal = 1` (opt-in, default off) | `hw_controller` and `delay_sync` | `delay_sync` returns to `STATE_INIT`, so a locked chain fully recalibrates. `heimdall-ctl recal` sends `RECL` and falls back to `INIT` when the server reports it disabled |
| Process restart | all | Full calibration |

`[calibration] recal_on_gain_change = 1` (opt-in, added in this release) recalibrates after a `GAIN` applied from port 5001, as `RECL` does (Section 7.3). It requires `en_wire_recal = 1` and is otherwise ignored with a warning. Scheduler gain changes never trigger it. A frequency change under the scheduler (`[schedule]`) uses the RF-change path. `hw_controller` also resets its burst counter on every scheduled `FREQ` command.

### 7.5 The calibration gain table

Calibration runs at a fixed gain per frequency band, not at the operating gain. `hw_controller.py` holds the table and picks the entry whose frequency is closest to `rf_center_freq`:

| Table frequency | 100 MHz | 200 MHz | 300 MHz | 400 MHz | 500 MHz | 600 MHz | 700 MHz | 1700 MHz |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gain index | 6 | 10 | 13 | 14 | 18 | 22 | 28 | 28 |
| Gain | 8.7 dB | 16.6 dB | 22.9 dB | 25.4 dB | 33.8 dB | 40.2 dB | 49.6 dB | 49.6 dB |

The docstring says the values were fitted to KerberosSDR v2 hardware. The table is not configurable. At the default 700 MHz, calibration runs at 49.6 dB while the default operating gain (`[daq] gain = 0`) is 0 dB. Any gain-dependent phase difference between the channels stays uncorrected. If your application needs the best phase accuracy, operate close to the calibration gain.

---

## 8. Gain budget: Friis noise figure and P1dB

`gain_budget.py` adds an advisory link budget for an external low-noise amplifier (LNA) placed before each tuner. It is enabled with `[amplification] en_amplification = 1`. It never changes a tuner gain. Its results are reported in header slots and on the `RFQ` query.

### 8.1 Total system gain

```
total_gain_db = antenna_gain_dbi − feed_loss_db + ext_lna_gain_db + tuner_gain_db
```

`feed_loss_db` is `cable_loss_db + connector_loss_db` from `[antenna]`. The tuner gain is the current R820T setting. The external LNA gain is continuous dB, held in a separate array. It never goes through the R820T gain table or into `if_gains[]`, because `hw_controller` compares `if_gains[]` against its own gain indices to decide when a gain change has taken effect.

### 8.2 Cascaded noise figure (Friis)

Noise figure (NF) measures how much a stage degrades the signal-to-noise ratio. In a chain of stages, the first stage dominates. Each later stage's contribution is divided by the total gain in front of it. That is the Friis formula, in linear units (noise factor `F = 10^(NF/10)`, gain `G = 10^(G_dB/10)`):

```
F_total = F1 + (F2 − 1)/G1 + (F3 − 1)/(G1 · G2) + ...
```

`gain_budget.py` models three stages: passive feed loss (gain `−L`, NF `L`), the external LNA, then the tuner (`tuner_nf_db`, default 3.5 dB). Antenna gain is a signal-only term and is not a noise stage.

Worked example:

| Chain | System NF |
|---|---|
| Tuner only (3.5 dB) | 3.5 dB |
| 2 dB of cable, then the tuner | 5.5 dB |
| 1 dB of cable, then an LNA with 20 dB gain and 0.8 dB NF, then the tuner | 1.84 dB |

The lesson is the usual one. Put the LNA as close to the antenna as possible, because loss in front of it adds directly to the noise figure. An external LNA sits outside the calibration point, because the noise source is injected after it. Its gain and phase differences between units are invisible to calibration. Measure them and put them into `iq_adjust` (Section 5.6), or use matched LNAs.

### 8.3 Compression headroom (P1dB)

An amplifier's 1 dB compression point (P1dB) is the output level at which its gain has dropped by 1 dB. Near that point the amplifier distorts, and its phase response changes with signal level. That breaks calibration in a way the noise source does not reveal.

```
estimated_output_dbm = expected_input_dbm + (ext_lna_gain_db − feed_loss_db)
headroom_db          = ext_lna_p1db_dbm − estimated_output_dbm
compressed           = headroom_db <= p1db_margin_db
```

`expected_input_dbm` is a static assumption from the INI (default −60 dBm), not a measurement. The header does not carry real per-sample input power. The compression flag is therefore an advisory. It is reported as its own per-channel bitmask (header slot 96, `compression_flags`) and as a warning event, and it never changes a gain. A P1dB of 99 dBm (the default) means "not modelled".

Source: `Firmware/_daq_core/gain_budget.py`, `Firmware/_daq_core/hw_controller.py` (`_update_link_budget`).

---

## 9. The IQ frame and header model

Every frame on every hop is a 1024-byte header followed by the payload. The header layout is defined in `Firmware/_daq_core/iq_header.h` and mirrored in `iq_header.py`. `protocols.md` has the byte-level table. This section explains what the fields mean for coherent processing.

### 9.1 Frame types

| Value | Name | Produced by | Payload | Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | DATA | `rtl_daq` while the noise source is off | `cpi_size` samples per channel at the output | Signal processing |
| 1 | DUMMY | `rtl_daq` for 5 frames after any command | none (`cpi_length = 0`) | Reset marker. Skip it |
| 2 | RAMP | Not produced by the chain. `_testing/unit_test/gen_ramp.py` writes ramp payloads as DATA frames by default and as type 2 only if asked | test pattern | Pipeline tests |
| 3 | CAL | `rtl_daq` while the noise source is on | `corr_size` samples per channel at the full rate | Calibration. Skip it for signal processing |
| 4 | TRIGW | defined in the header files, not produced by the chain | none | Reserved |

### 9.2 CPI

A coherent processing interval (CPI) is the block of samples that a DSP algorithm processes as one unit. In this chain one DATA frame is one CPI. `cpi_size` counts samples after decimation, so the chain collects `cpi_size × decimation_ratio` ADC samples per frame. `ini_checker.py` requires `cpi_size × decimation_ratio >= daq_buffer_size`. It does not require `corr_size <= cpi_size` (the old check is disabled). `delay_sync` uses the whole DATA frame when `cpi_size < corr_size`.

### 9.3 Fields that matter for coherence

| Field | Writer | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `frame_type` | rtl_daq | See 9.1 |
| `rf_center_freq` | rtl_daq | Current LO frequency. A change means the LO phases are new |
| `adc_sampling_freq`, `sampling_freq` | rtl_daq, decimate | ADC rate, and output rate after decimation |
| `cpi_length` | rebuffer, decimate | Samples per channel in this frame |
| `time_stamp` | rtl_daq, corrected by rebuffer | Milliseconds since the Unix epoch, wall clock (`gettimeofday`), with millisecond resolution |
| `daq_block_index` | rtl_daq | DAQ block counter at the source |
| `cpi_index` | decimate | Frame counter at the decimator, DUMMY frames included. A gap means a frame was lost downstream of it |
| `if_gains[32]` | rtl_daq | Tuner gain per channel, tenths of a dB |
| `adc_overdrive_flags` | rtl_daq, ORed by rebuffer | Bit `m` is set when any I or Q byte of channel `m` equals 255 (positive full scale). Negative-rail clipping (code 0) is not detected. Clipping distorts the phase |
| `noise_source_state` | rtl_daq | 1 while the noise source is on |
| `delay_sync_flag` | delay_sync | Sample alignment holds (Section 6) |
| `iq_sync_flag` | delay_sync | Amplitude and phase calibration holds |
| `sync_state` | delay_sync | State machine value 0 to 6 (Section 6) |
| `reserved[102]` | rtl_daq | Cumulative USB ring overrun count. An increase means coherence is not guaranteed for that frame |
| `header_version` | rtl_daq | 8 |

Header version 8 also names slots 0 to 101 of `reserved[]` for RF front-end and orientation telemetry: external LNA gains, total system gains, system NF, compression and bias-tee bitmasks, antenna bearing, rotator state and the aggregate channel power. `delay_sync` stamps these when the front-end telemetry is enabled. `iq_header.h` also defines slots 103 to 113 for opt-in router, node and calibration telemetry. Slots 103 to 113 stay zero unless their opt-in key or flag is set. Slot 106 encodes `instance_id + 1`, so zero there means untagged. In slots 0 to 102 a zero can be a real value (no compression, bias tees off, azimuth 0 = north, no overruns), so check the enabling config rather than treating zero as missing.

### 9.4 Time stamps

`time_stamp` is a host wall-clock reading. It is taken when `rtl_daq` has received a block from every channel, so it includes USB and scheduling latency. Rebuffer back-dates it by the age of the samples left in its buffer, so it marks the arrival of the frame's last sample. The frame's first sample is about 437 ms earlier at the defaults (`cpi_size × decimation_ratio / adc_sampling_freq`). Its resolution is 1 ms, which is 2400 samples at 2.4 MS/s. NTP can step or slew it. Use `cpi_index` and `daq_block_index`, not `time_stamp`, to detect lost frames. Use `time_stamp` only to relate frames to wall-clock events, and only to millisecond accuracy.

---

## 10. Limits: coherent islands and federation

**Point:** coherence exists only inside one unit, which means one enclosure, one `rtl_daq` process and one `delay_sync` process. Two units are two independent "coherent islands". Nothing in this firmware makes them coherent with each other.

### 10.1 Why separate units are not coherent

Every mechanism in Sections 2 to 7 is local to one island:

| Mechanism | Scope |
|---|---|
| Reference oscillator | One per enclosure |
| Noise source | One per enclosure, on GPIO 0 of that unit's control dongle |
| Block alignment by transfer count | Inside one `rtl_daq` process |
| Delay and IQ calibration | Inside one `delay_sync` process, against that unit's reference channel |
| Rate nudges | Sent by one `delay_sync` to its own `rtl_daq` |

Between two enclosures, every impairment from Section 2.2 is back, and two more appear:

- **Frequency offset.** Two crystals differ by some parts per million. A 1 ppm difference at 700 MHz is a 700 Hz beat. The phase between the two units turns a full circle every 1.4 ms. No constant correction can remove that.
- **Time base.** The only common time between units is `time_stamp`, a millisecond wall clock. One millisecond is 2400 samples, and at the speed of light it is 300 km. Even with good NTP or PTP discipline of the hosts, this aligns frames, not samples.

Feeding two units from one external reference and one external noise source does not fix this either. The firmware calibrates each island separately against its own reference channel. Nothing estimates the delay or phase between islands.

### 10.2 Federation does not create coherence

Federation (`[federation]`, `federation_coordinator.py`, `federation_iq_router.py`) coordinates several instances. It can fan out frequency and gain commands, split a frequency plan, collect health and events, and merge IQ streams. By default the router writes the source instance into the header `unit_id` field. This release adds opt-in tag modes (`--tag-mode unit|node`) that keep `unit_id` and use reserved slots 106/107 instead. The router's optional `time_stamp` alignment window (`--align-window-ms`) groups frames from different units by wall-clock milliseconds. It does not align samples between sources, does not correct phase, and does not make the units coherent. A merged stream is a set of independent island streams side by side.

Calibration bursts are also not synchronised across instances. Each `hw_controller` counts its own frames to its own `cal_frame_interval`. Two instances on the same frequency have no guaranteed common DATA window.

### 10.3 What this means for multi-unit applications

| Application | Works across units? | How |
|---|---|---|
| Per-unit DoA, then triangulation | Yes | Each island computes a bearing. Fuse the bearings with the unit positions and orientations |
| Wide-band or multi-frequency survey | Yes | Assign frequencies per unit (federation partitioning) |
| Detection or power fusion | Yes | Combine per-unit results non-coherently |
| Time difference of arrival (TDOA) | No | Needs sample-level common time. `time_stamp` gives 1 ms |
| One large coherent array or beamformer across enclosures | No | Needs a common clock, a common noise reference and joint calibration in one process |
| Passive radar with reference and surveillance in different units | No | Needs a common frequency reference and sample-level alignment |

A larger coherent array needs hardware that shares the clock and the noise source across all its tuners, driven by one `rtl_daq` and one `delay_sync`. The firmware supports at most 31 coherent channels. The 128-byte ZMQ control messages carry 31 per-channel values (`ZMQ_MAX_CH_PARAMS` in `rtl_daq.c`), so a 32nd channel could never receive a rate correction. `rtl_daq` rejects `num_ch > 31` (`device_map_resolve()`: "num_ch out of range 1..31", `DEVICE_MAP_MAX_CH` in `device_map.h`), and `ini_checker` rejects it as well (`MAX_NUM_CH = 31`). Coherence at that size also depends on the hardware sharing one clock and one noise source across all tuners.

Comparing `time_stamp` across hosts needs disciplined clocks (NTP at least, PTP for better accuracy) on every host. See [networking_and_time_sync.md](networking_and_time_sync.html).

---

## 11. Constants reference

Hard-coded values that shape calibration behaviour. None of them is configurable from the INI. The two USB depths that used to be the constants `NUM_BUFF` and `ASYNC_BUF_NUMBER` are now INI keys; they are listed in the next table.

| Constant | Value | Where | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `NO_DUMMY_FRAMES` | 5 | `rtl_daq.c` | DUMMY frames after each command |
| `FS_CORRECTION_KEEP_LIMIT` | 0.008 | `rtl_daq.c` | Rate corrections at or above this stay active |
| `min_corr_peak_dyn_range` | 20 dB | `delay_sync.py` | Correlation peak-to-sidelobe gate |
| `corr_peak_offset` | 100 samples | `delay_sync.py` | Sidelobe probe lag |
| `MIN_FS_PPM_OFFSET` | 1e-7 | `delay_sync.py` | Unit of the rate correction |
| `MAX_FS_PPM_OFFSET` | 0.01 | `delay_sync.py` | Clip for the integer-stage correction |
| `INT_FS_TUNE_GAIN` | 50 / 25 / 15 for `|d|` ≥ 100 / ≥ 2 / below 2 | `delay_sync.py` | Integer-stage loop gains |
| `FRAC_FS_TUNE_GAIN` | 20 | `delay_sync.py` | Fractional-stage loop gain |
| `frac_delay_tolerance` | 0.03 samples | `delay_sync.py` | Fractional stage done below this |
| Fractional FFT block | 1024 samples | `delay_sync.py` | `estimate_frac_delays` block size |
| Fractional fit band | `−0.4 < f < 0.4` | `delay_sync.py` | Normalised frequencies used for the slope fit |
| `cal_gain_table` | Section 7.5 | `hw_controller.py` | Calibration gain per band |
| uint8 to float | `(x − 127.5) / 127.5` | `offload_cpu_generic.c` | ADC code to [−1, 1] |

INI keys that control calibration, with defaults (see [configuration.md](configuration.html) for the full description):

| Key | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `[daq] en_noise_source_ctr` | 1 | Switch the noise-source GPIO |
| `[daq] ctr_channel_serial_no` | 1000 | Dongle that drives the noise source and bias tees |
| `[daq] usb_ring_buffers` | 8 | Ring slots per channel, 2 to 64. Lapping the ring is an overrun |
| `[daq] usb_async_transfers` | 12 | librtlsdr async transfer buffers per device, 2 to 64 |
| `[calibration] corr_size` | 65536 | CAL frame length and correlation size |
| `[calibration] std_ch_ind` | 0 | Reference channel |
| `[calibration] en_iq_cal` | 1 | Apply DC removal and amplitude/phase correction |
| `[calibration] amplitude_cal_mode` | `channel_power` | `default`, `disabled` or `channel_power` |
| `[calibration] cal_track_mode` | 2 | 0, 1 or 2 (Section 7.1) |
| `[calibration] cal_frame_interval` | 687 | Frames in `sync_state` 6 between bursts |
| `[calibration] cal_frame_burst_size` | 10 | Frames per burst |
| `[calibration] maximum_sync_fails` | 10 | Net failures in a burst that drop the lock |
| `[calibration] amplitude_tolerance` | 2 | dB, integer |
| `[calibration] phase_tolerance` | 1 | degrees, integer |
| `[calibration] require_track_lock_intervention` | 0 | After each full calibration (start-up, retune, lock loss), wait for a `1` in `_data_control/iq_track_lock` (`inst{N}_iq_track_lock` for N > 0) before switching the noise source off. Not applied to periodic mode-2 bursts. The file is not cleared, so a `1` stays an approval |
| `[calibration] iq_adjust_source` | `explicit-time-delay` | Or `touchstone` |
| `[calibration] iq_adjust_amplitude` | `0,0,0,0` | dB per non-reference channel |
| `[calibration] iq_adjust_time_delay_ns` | `0, 0, 0, 0` | ns per non-reference channel |
| `[calibration] en_gain_tune_init` | 0 | Raise gains until overdrive at start-up |
| `[calibration] gain_lock_interval` | 0 | Frames without change before gain tuning is done |
| `[calibration] unified_gain_control` | 0 | Force the same gain on all channels (the minimum) |

## 12. Further reading

- Mikko Laakso, "Multichannel coherent receiver on the RTL-SDR", Master's thesis, Aalto University, 2019. The fractional-delay-by-rate-tuning method used here. `delay_sync.py` cites it.
- T. I. Laakso, V. Välimäki, M. Karjalainen, U. K. Laine, "Splitting the unit delay: tools for fractional delay filter design", IEEE Signal Processing Magazine, 1996.
- C. H. Knapp, G. C. Carter, "The generalized correlation method for estimation of time delay", IEEE Transactions on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing, 1976.
- H. L. Van Trees, "Optimum Array Processing" (Detection, Estimation, and Modulation Theory, Part IV), Wiley, 2002.
- H. Krim, M. Viberg, "Two decades of array signal processing research: the parametric approach", IEEE Signal Processing Magazine, 1996.
- R. O. Schmidt, "Multiple emitter location and signal parameter estimation", IEEE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation, 1986.
- A. Paulraj, T. Kailath, "Direction of arrival estimation by eigenstructure methods with unknown sensor gain and phase", Proceedings of ICASSP, 1985.
- H. T. Friis, "Noise figures of radio receivers", Proceedings of the IRE, 1944.
- H. D. Griffiths, C. J. Baker, "An Introduction to Passive Radar", Artech House, 2017.
- R. G. Lyons, "Understanding Digital Signal Processing", Prentice Hall. FIR filters, windowing and decimation.
- `Documentation/HDAQ_firmware_ver1.0.20201130.pdf`, the original 2020 firmware documentation. It is historical, so use it for background only.
